name: Retrieval practice
description: People pull an answer, a procedure or a decision out of their own memory instead of reading it again. The act of recalling it makes it easier to recall next time, and it shows both of you what is not there yet.
what: Each time someone recalls something with effort, the route back to it gets stronger. Re-reading feels easier but does much less. Recall followed by the right answer also corrects what people got wrong.
basis: Roediger and Karpicke (2006), test-enhanced learning; Rowland (2014), a meta-analysis of the testing effect; Dunlosky and colleagues (2013), a review of ten study techniques, which rated practice testing among the most useful.
methods: Retrieval practice; Flashcards and quiz cards; Teach-back; Successive relearning; Scenario-based learning
example: Open the second morning with notes closed: "Write down the four steps of the feedback model and one thing that goes wrong at each." Give three minutes, then show the answer and let people mark their own.
useful: Knowledge, steps and language people must produce at work without looking them up.
failures: Questions that test trivia rather than what the job needs; recall that only asks people to recognise an answer from a list; high-stakes tests that make people anxious; no correct answer given afterwards
checks: Do people have to produce the answer without seeing it? Is it low stakes, repeated over time and followed by the right answer?

name: Spacing
description: People meet the same material several times with gaps in between, instead of all at once. A little forgetting between sessions makes the next recall harder, and the learning lasts longer for it.
what: Coming back to something after a gap makes people rebuild it, which strengthens it more than another go straight away. The right gap depends on how long they need to remember it.
basis: Cepeda and colleagues (2006), a review of 271 comparisons of spaced and massed study; Cepeda and colleagues (2008), on how the best gap depends on how long you need to remember.
methods: Spaced practice; Nudges and reminders; Successive relearning; Microlearning; Blended learning
example: Teach a conversation model on day one. Ask for it from memory at the start of day two, use it in a practice call in week one back at work, and run a 30-minute clinic on it in week four.
useful: Anything people need to remember well after the course, especially where forgetting is costly.
failures: Reminders that ask people to read again instead of recall or use; repeating the same content word for word; gaps chosen for diary convenience with no thought for when the skill will be needed
checks: Do people meet the key ideas at least three times, spread out? Does each meeting ask them to recall or use it?

name: Interleaving
description: Related problem types, cases or skills are mixed in one practice set, so people have to work out which kind of situation they face before they respond. The opposite is blocked practice, one type at a time. Mixing the order of practice for physical and spoken routines, known as contextual interference, works the same way.
what: When the type of problem is not announced, people practise spotting which approach fits as well as carrying it out. Practice feels harder and looks worse on the day, and is remembered and used better later.
basis: Brunmair and Richter (2019), a meta-analysis of interleaved learning, which found the benefit depends on how similar the types are; Rohrer and Taylor (2007), on mixed maths practice; Shea and Morgan (1979), the first study of contextual interference in motor learning.
methods: Interleaved practice; Scenario-based learning; Role-play; Simulation-based training
example: After teaching three ways to handle a complaint separately, give six short cases in a random order. For each, people first say which approach fits and why, then play it.
useful: Judgement and diagnosis, where the hard part is recognising which situation you are in.
failures: Mixing before people can do each type on its own; mixing types that are so different there is nothing to tell apart; judging the method by how the practice round looked
checks: Do people have to choose the approach, or are they told? Are the mixed types similar enough to be confused?

name: Generation
description: People try to produce an answer, an explanation or a plan before they are given one. Even a poor first attempt gives the teaching that follows something to attach to.
what: Having a go brings what people already know to mind and shows them where the gaps are. What people produce themselves is remembered better than what they read.
basis: Slamecka and Graf (1978), the generation effect; Fiorella and Mayer (2016), eight ways to promote generative learning; Richland, Kornell and Kao (2009), on how attempting a question before study helps later recall.
methods: Teach-back; Concept mapping; Problem-based learning; Flipped learning
example: Before you teach how to write a discovery question, pairs write the five best questions they can for a messy client brief. Then show an expert set and have them mark what theirs missed.
useful: Waking up what people already know and making the teaching that follows land.
failures: Asking for wild guesses about things people have no way to know; showing up a beginner in front of the group; never comparing what they produced with a correct version
checks: Is it safe to get it wrong? Does a correct explanation and a second attempt always follow?

name: Productive failure
description: People attempt a hard, open problem before they are taught how to solve it. Most attempts fall short. The teaching that follows then uses those attempts to show what the good solution does differently.
what: Struggling first shows people the limits of what they know and makes them ready for the explanation. It only works when the teaching comes straight after and builds on their attempts.
basis: Kapur (2008), on productive failure; Sinha and Kapur (2021), a meta-analysis of 53 studies of problem solving before instruction, which found a moderate benefit when the design followed productive-failure principles and the learners had some background.
methods: Problem-based learning; Challenge-based learning; Case method
example: Teams draft a rollout plan for a new tool with no guidance. They put the plans on the wall, you group the common gaps, then teach a readiness checklist and they redo the plan.
useful: Understanding why a method works, and experienced groups who would otherwise coast.
failures: An attempt with no teaching afterwards; a problem so far beyond people that there is nothing to try; singling someone out; treating struggle as the goal
checks: Can people make a real start on the problem? Does structured teaching follow straight away, with a second attempt?

name: Desirable difficulty
description: The umbrella idea behind spacing, interleaving, generation and recall: some kinds of effort slow people down in the session but make learning last. A difficulty is only useful if people can still succeed with effort.
what: Practice that feels smooth often fades quickly. Practice that makes people work to recall or choose builds stronger, more flexible memory, even though it feels less fluent.
basis: Bjork (1994), on desirable difficulties; Bjork and Bjork (2011), on making things hard on yourself in a good way; Soderstrom and Bjork (2015), on the difference between performance in training and learning.
methods: Spaced practice; Interleaved practice; Retrieval practice; Faded worked examples
example: After two guided rehearsals of a pitch, give people a new audience they have not prepared for and take the slide template away. Tell them first that this round is meant to feel harder.
useful: Making skills last and travel, once people have the basics.
failures: Adding complexity for drama; overwhelming beginners; treating frustration as a sign of learning; not telling people why it feels hard, so they give up on it
checks: What useful mental work does the difficulty force? Can people still succeed with effort and some support?

name: Elaboration
description: People connect new ideas to what they already know by asking why and how, finding their own examples and drawing comparisons.
what: Each meaningful connection gives another way back to the idea, and trying to explain why something works shows up shallow understanding.
basis: Pressley and colleagues (1987), on asking why; Dunlosky and colleagues (2013), which rated elaborative interrogation as moderately useful; Craik and Lockhart (1972), levels of processing.
methods: Concept mapping; Peer instruction; Case method; Teach-back
example: After a short input on why prototypes reduce risk, each person writes one example from their own work where a prototype would have saved time, and one where it would not have helped, then explains both to a partner.
useful: Understanding ideas well enough to apply them, and joining new ideas to people's existing expertise.
failures: Open discussion with no structure; explanations that sound right but are wrong; connections that drift away from the task the course is for
checks: Do the prompts ask why and when it does not apply? Is anyone checking the explanations are right?

name: Self-explanation
description: People explain to themselves or a partner why each step of an example or their own work was done, including the options they rejected.
what: Putting the reasoning into words makes people join up the steps, notice what they do not understand and bring hidden assumptions into the open.
basis: Chi and colleagues (1989), on self-explanations in learning from examples; Bisra and colleagues (2018), a meta-analysis of self-explanation, which found a moderate benefit.
methods: Worked examples; Expert think-aloud; Learning journal; Studio learning / design critique
example: Hand out a strong sample proposal. Each person annotates three choices in the margin: what the writer did, why, and what they could have done instead. Then compare notes in pairs.
useful: Complex reasoning, learning a procedure from an example and surfacing assumptions people do not know they hold.
failures: Describing what was done without saying why; explanations nobody checks; asking people to talk through their reasoning while they are under pressure to perform
checks: Are people explaining reasons and alternatives, not just actions? Is the explaining kept apart from high-pressure performance?

name: Dual coding
description: An idea is shown in words and in a picture that explains it, such as a diagram, a map or a timeline, so people build two linked versions of it. The picture has to carry meaning, not decorate the slide.
what: Words and a meaningful picture give two routes into memory. They work best when the picture shows structure the words describe, without adding a third stream to read.
basis: Paivio (1971), dual coding theory; Mayer (2020), Multimedia Learning, third edition, on learning from words and pictures together.
methods: Interactive lecture; Concept mapping; Interactive video
example: Build a process map on the flipchart box by box while you explain it, instead of showing the finished slide. At the end of the session, people redraw it from memory.
useful: Processes, systems, cause and effect, and anything with a shape.
failures: Decorative stock images; dense text on screen read out at the same time; diagrams so busy they compete with the speaker
checks: Does the picture explain something the words alone would not? Can people look at it and listen at the same time?

name: Cognitive load management
description: The design controls how much new information people have to hold in mind at once. Complex material is broken down and sequenced, and anything that adds effort without teaching is cut.
what: Working memory can hold only a few new things at a time. Once ideas are learned they take up less room, which is why what is too much for a beginner can be too little for an expert.
basis: Sweller (1988), cognitive load theory; Cowan (2001), on a working memory limit of about four chunks; Kalyuga (2007), on the expertise reversal effect.
methods: Worked examples; Faded worked examples; Job aids and in-tool guidance; Microlearning
example: For a new booking system, people first watch one booking done end to end, then finish a half-completed booking, and only then do a full one alone. The reference details stay on a printed card.
useful: Beginners, complex subjects and any course with dense or unfamiliar content.
failures: Slides crammed with text; several instructions given at once; extra technology that people must learn before they can learn the subject; keeping heavy support for people who no longer need it
checks: What must people hold in their heads at each point? What could go on a card or a screen instead?

name: Scaffolding and fading
description: Temporary support, such as a template, a prompt or a coach at the shoulder, helps people do more than they could alone. The support is taken away step by step as they improve.
what: Support lowers the load early on. Removing it makes people recall and decide for themselves, which is what they will have to do at work.
basis: Wood, Bruner and Ross (1976), the origin of the term scaffolding; Renkl and Atkinson (2003), on fading worked examples; Collins, Brown and Newman (1989), cognitive apprenticeship.
methods: Faded worked examples; Cognitive apprenticeship; Job instruction training; Coaching
example: Round one of a coaching practice uses a card with all five questions. Round two uses a card with the first word of each. Round three uses no card.
useful: Moving people from first attempts to doing it alone.
failures: Support that is never removed; support pulled away all at once; generic templates that do the thinking for people
checks: Does each support meet a real need? What will tell you it is time to remove it?

name: Worked-example learning
description: People study a complete, good solution, including the reasoning behind it, before they try similar problems themselves.
what: Studying a solved example lets beginners see the structure and the choices, instead of using up their limited working memory searching for an answer.
basis: Sweller and Cooper (1985), the worked-example effect; Barbieri and colleagues (2023), a meta-analysis of worked examples in maths; Kalyuga (2007), on why the benefit fades as people gain expertise.
methods: Worked examples; Faded worked examples; Expert think-aloud; Demonstration then imitation
example: Walk through a strong client proposal and label the evidence, the assumptions, the trade-offs and what was left out. Then people draft one section of their own using the same labels.
useful: Beginners facing complex tasks with a clear structure.
failures: Showing only the polished result and hiding the reasoning; example after example with no practice; using full examples with experts who would learn more from a problem
checks: Does the example show the decisions as well as the result? Does practice follow straight after?

name: Contrast and variation
description: People compare carefully chosen examples side by side, such as good and poor versions, or cases that differ in one way that matters. The difference makes the important feature easy to see.
what: It is hard to see what makes something good from a single example. Putting two close examples together shows which feature makes the difference.
basis: Alfieri, Nokes-Malach and Schunn (2013), a meta-analysis of learning through comparing cases; Gentner (1983), structure-mapping; Marton (2015), variation theory.
methods: Studio learning / design critique; Case method; Demonstration then imitation
example: Play two recordings of the same difficult call, one handled well and one handled poorly. Before you say anything, pairs list the three differences that mattered most.
useful: Judging quality, and ideas people tend to treat as a checklist.
failures: Examples that differ in so many ways the key difference is lost; showing a poor example without saying why it fails
checks: Are the examples close enough for the key difference to stand out? Do people have to put the difference into words?

name: Feedback
description: Information that shows people the gap between what they did and the goal, and what to do next. The same idea, aimed forward at the next attempt, is often called feedforward. Good feedback is specific, about the task and followed by another go.
what: People adjust when they get credible information about the task and a chance to act on it. Feedback about the person, or with no next step, does little and can make things worse. When to give it depends on the task: correct early for beginners and for safety, and let more experienced people finish an attempt and judge it themselves first.
basis: Hattie and Timperley (2007), the power of feedback; Kluger and DeNisi (1996), a meta-analysis showing that about a third of feedback interventions made performance worse; Shute (2008), on the timing of feedback.
methods: Coaching; Practice clinic; Role-play; Peer coaching; After-action review
example: After a practice call, name one thing that worked and one thing to change, framed for next time: "In the next call, pause after you state the problem and ask what they have seen." Then they run that moment again straight away.
useful: Refining any skill you can observe against a clear standard.
failures: Vague praise; too many points at once; comments about the person rather than the task; no chance to try again; interrupting so often that people never complete an attempt; leaving a beginner to repeat an error for too long
checks: Is the feedback tied to what you saw and to a standard? Does the person know the next action and get to try it?

name: Metacognitive calibration
description: People compare how well they think they know or can do something with how well they actually do. Predicting a score and then seeing the real one shows them where they are over or under confident.
what: People are often poor judges of their own learning, and easy study makes them feel they know more than they do. Repeatedly checking predictions against results helps them judge better and choose what to practise next.
basis: Dunlosky and Rawson (2012), on overconfidence and poor study choices; Zell and Krizan (2014), a review finding only moderate links between people's ratings of their own ability and their performance; Kornell and Bjork (2008), on how people misjudge spacing.
methods: Flashcards and quiz cards; Learning journal; Mock assessment centre
example: Before a scored practice conversation, each person writes down the score they expect out of ten. Afterwards they compare it with the observer's score and note the one thing they did not notice they were missing.
useful: Professional judgement, learning on your own and spotting false confidence.
failures: Reflection with no evidence to check against; treating confidence as competence; ranking people publicly
checks: Is there a prediction and a real result to compare? Do people use the gap to choose what to practise next?

name: Goal setting
description: A clear, challenging goal focuses attention and effort and gives people a standard to check themselves against. For new, complex tasks a goal about learning the method works better than a goal about the result.
what: Specific goals make people try harder and keep going, especially with feedback. When a task is new and complex, a hard result goal can push people to rush instead of learning how to do it.
basis: Locke and Latham (2002), goal-setting theory; Seijts and Latham (2001), on learning goals for complex tasks.
methods: Deliberate practice; Coaching; Stretch assignment; Portfolio-based learning and assessment
example: At the start of a practice day, each person writes one learning goal they can check by the end: "In the last role-play I will ask three questions before I suggest anything."
useful: Practice, behaviour change and projects that run over weeks.
failures: Vague goals; too many goals at once; result targets for things people do not control; competitive goals that discourage trying new approaches
checks: Is the goal specific, observable and challenging? Will people get feedback against it?

name: Implementation intentions
description: People write a plan in the form "When this happens, I will do that", linking a real situation at work to a specific action.
what: Naming the situation in advance means it triggers the action with less thought when it comes. It closes part of the gap between meaning to do something and doing it.
basis: Gollwitzer and Sheeran (2006), a meta-analysis of 94 studies of if-then plans, which found a medium to large effect on reaching goals. Most of the studies were in health, study and laboratory settings.
methods: Learning journal; Coaching; Nudges and reminders
example: In the last half hour, each person writes: "When a client asks for a price before the problem is clear, I will say what I have understood so far and ask what they have tried." Their partner checks it names a real moment.
useful: Turning a good intention from the course into action back at work.
failures: Plans with no real trigger; too many plans; plans for actions the workplace makes impossible
checks: Is the situation specific and likely to happen soon? Is the action within the person's control?

name: Deliberate practice
description: Practice aimed at one specific part of a skill, just beyond what someone can do now, against a clear standard, with expert feedback and repeated with a change each time.
what: Focused repetition with correction refines how people do the hard part, until it runs without much thought. Hours of practice alone explain less than the slogans suggest. The quality of the practice matters.
basis: Ericsson, Krampe and Tesch-Römer (1993), the original deliberate practice study; Macnamara, Hambrick and Oswald (2014), a meta-analysis finding practice explains a modest share of performance, and very little in professions.
methods: Deliberate practice; Practice clinic; Role-play; Coaching
example: Instead of running a whole sales call, each person practises only the move from questions to recommendation, six times, with the buyer reacting differently each time and a coach giving one point after each.
useful: Skills you can break into parts, watch and repeat.
failures: Repeating without thinking; always practising the whole task without finding the weak part; no clear standard; people too tired to concentrate
checks: Which part exactly is being improved? Is the feedback expert enough, and does each attempt change something?

name: Variability of practice
description: People practise the same skill in different situations, with different people or under different conditions, so they learn the principle and not one script.
what: Varied practice helps people see what stays the same underneath the surface, which helps them use the skill in situations the course did not cover.
basis: Schmidt (1975), schema theory of motor learning; Barnett and Ceci (2002), on what makes transfer near or far.
methods: Scenario-based learning; Role-play; Simulation-based training
example: Each person gives the same two-minute pitch three times: to a keen sponsor, a sceptical finance director and a technical expert. Afterwards they list what they kept the same and what they changed.
useful: Using a skill flexibly, once people have the basic pattern.
failures: Varying before people can do the basic version; changing things that have nothing to do with the skill
checks: What should stay the same across rounds, and what should change?

name: Overlearning and automaticity
description: Practice continues after people first get it right, so the most-used parts become automatic and take less attention.
what: Once the routine parts run on their own, people have attention free for judgement and the unexpected. The benefit fades over time without use.
basis: Driskell, Willis and Copper (1992), a meta-analysis of overlearning; Anderson (1982), on how skills become automatic.
methods: Retrieval practice; Job instruction training; Flashcards and quiz cards
example: People practise the first 30 seconds of a client call until they can give it accurately without notes, so their attention in the real call goes to what the client says.
useful: Safety routines, basic procedures and short, frequent moves such as an opening line.
failures: Drilling a script until it sounds robotic; using it for complex judgement; going on past the point of benefit
checks: Will making this automatic free attention for harder work? Is variation added afterwards?

name: Observational learning
description: People learn by watching someone else do it, noticing what happens as a result, and then trying it themselves.
what: Watching a credible model shows what good looks like and how it is done. People learn most when they are told what to look for and practise soon after.
basis: Bandura (1977), social learning theory; Taylor, Russ-Eft and Chan (2005), a meta-analysis of behaviour modelling training.
methods: Demonstration then imitation; Shadowing; Fishbowl discussion; Expert think-aloud
example: Two facilitators handle the same objection in different ways in front of the group. People note what each noticed and said, then try both approaches in pairs.
useful: People skills, procedures and craft skills.
failures: Watching with no task; a model so expert nobody could copy them; no practice afterwards
checks: Are people told what to watch for? Do they try it soon after watching?

name: Cognitive apprenticeship
description: An expert makes their thinking visible on real tasks: they show and explain, then coach, then step back as the learner takes over.
what: Experts often cannot see their own decisions any more. Thinking aloud on real work lets learners pick up the judgement as well as the steps.
basis: Collins, Brown and Newman (1989), cognitive apprenticeship; Clark and colleagues (2008), on cognitive task analysis and the expert blind spot.
methods: Cognitive apprenticeship; Expert think-aloud; Shadowing; Apprenticeship; Coaching
example: An experienced consultant runs the first client discovery call and talks through her choices afterwards. She coaches the learner through the second, then watches the learner run the third alone.
useful: Complex work where the judgement is usually hidden.
failures: Expert monologues; too little real practice; never stepping back; experts who cannot explain what has become automatic for them
checks: Are showing, coaching, explaining and stepping back all there?

name: Situated learning
description: Learning happens in, or close to, the place, tools and people where the work is done, and people learn by taking part in real work.
what: Knowledge is tied to the setting where it is used. Taking part in real work builds the skill and a sense of belonging to the profession.
basis: Lave and Wenger (1991), situated learning and legitimate peripheral participation; Brown, Collins and Duguid (1989), situated cognition.
methods: Live case; On-the-job training; Apprenticeship; Community of practice; Field study / contextual immersion
example: Instead of an invented case, teams work on a real client brief, with the real constraints and the tools they will use to deliver it, and present to the person who owns it.
useful: Skills that depend on context and role.
failures: Assuming realism alone teaches; passing on bad local habits; real situations too complex for beginners
checks: Which parts of the real setting matter for the skill? Where do guidance and reflection happen?

name: Transfer-appropriate practice
description: Practice asks people to notice and decide the same things the job will ask of them. What matters is the decision, not how real the setting looks.
what: People recall and use learning best when the practice and the job ask for the same kind of thinking.
basis: Morris, Bransford and Franks (1977), transfer-appropriate processing; Thorndike and Woodworth (1901), identical elements.
methods: Simulation-based training; Scenario-based learning; Live case; Role-play
example: If the job means pushing back on a senior person when the facts are unclear, the practice is a role-play with an unclear brief and a senior person, not a quiz on the model.
useful: High-stakes work and closing the gap between knowing and doing.
failures: Paying for realistic-looking simulations that ask for the wrong decisions; teaching knowledge when the job needs action
checks: Does the practice contain the same cues, pressures and decisions as the job?

name: Near and far transfer
description: Near transfer is using learning in situations like the course. Far transfer is applying the principle somewhere quite different. Far transfer rarely happens on its own. Comparing two or more examples, and saying what they share, helps people carry a principle across, which is also how analogies work.
what: People tend to notice surface features. To apply a principle somewhere new, they must see the deeper structure the two situations share and know where the comparison breaks down.
basis: Barnett and Ceci (2002), a taxonomy of transfer; Gick and Holyoak (1983), on analogical transfer and the value of comparing two examples; Blume and colleagues (2010), a meta-analysis of transfer of training at work.
methods: Case method; Scenario-based learning; Action learning sets
example: Teams use a discovery method on a technology brief, then on a reorganisation. They finish by writing what stayed the same, what changed and where the method would not fit.
useful: Skills expected to work across clients, markets or roles.
failures: Assuming an inspiring event will transfer; jumping straight to very different settings; never naming the shared principle; comparisons that carry over wrong assumptions
checks: Is near transfer secure first? Do people compare settings and state the shared principle, and its limits?

name: Social learning and co-construction
description: People build understanding by explaining, arguing and making things together. In the structured form, each person commits to an answer alone, discusses it with peers, then answers again.
what: Explaining your reasoning to someone else shows its gaps, and hearing another view can shift a misunderstanding. Committing alone first stops the loudest voice deciding for everyone.
basis: Crouch and Mazur (2001), ten years of peer instruction; Smith and colleagues (2009), on why peer discussion improves understanding; Kobayashi (2019), a meta-analysis of learning by teaching.
methods: Peer instruction; Learning by teaching; Reciprocal teaching; World Café; Case method
example: Show a case and ask everyone to write which assumption is riskiest. Then trios argue their choice for four minutes, everyone votes again, and only then do you give your view.
useful: Ambiguous problems, misunderstandings and seeing other points of view.
failures: Dominant voices; groupthink; people leaving the work to others; agreement with no evidence; questions too easy to argue about
checks: Does everyone think alone before the discussion? Is there real disagreement to work through?

name: Psychological safety for learning
description: People feel safe enough to ask questions, admit what they do not know, disagree and try hard things without being punished or embarrassed. Safety is not comfort, and it does not mean lower standards.
what: When people do not fear looking foolish, they speak up, try things, report mistakes and ask for help. Those are the behaviours learning depends on.
basis: Edmondson (1999), on psychological safety and learning behaviour in work teams; Frazier and colleagues (2017), a meta-analysis of psychological safety at work.
methods: Fishbowl discussion; Action learning sets; Peer coaching
example: The most senior person in the room goes first in the difficult role-play, says afterwards what they found hard and asks for one specific piece of feedback.
useful: Practising with people, new ideas, mixed groups and learning from mistakes.
failures: Calling it a safe space without changing who holds power in the room; forcing people to share personal things; avoiding all challenge
checks: Can people decline an activity or choose another way in? Are the rules on feedback and recording clear?

name: Social accountability
description: People make a commitment to peers, a coach or their group, and the group meets again to look at what happened.
what: Knowing others will ask can help people follow through. It works when the commitment is realistic and support comes with it.
basis: Harkin and colleagues (2016), a meta-analysis finding that monitoring progress, especially when it is reported or made public, helps people reach goals.
methods: Peer coaching; Action learning sets; Cohort-based course
example: Each person names one thing they will try at work and brings evidence of how it went to the next meeting of their trio in three weeks.
useful: Keeping practice going after the course and finishing projects.
failures: Public promises with no support; shaming people who did not manage it; going through the motions; peers who cannot remove the real obstacles
checks: Is the commitment within the person's control and checkable? Is there support as well as checking?

name: Autonomy and choice
description: People have real choices about goals, routes, examples or methods, within clear limits. Choice should make the learning more relevant, not leave people facing a long menu.
what: Having some control raises motivation and ownership, especially when people also feel capable and connected to others.
basis: Deci and Ryan (2000), self-determination theory; Patall, Cooper and Robinson (2008), a meta-analysis of the effects of choice.
methods: Open Space Technology; Cohort-based course; Stretch assignment
example: Everyone takes the shared morning on client basics. In the afternoon, people choose between practice sessions on negotiation, facilitation or presenting.
useful: Experienced adults, mixed groups and programmes that need people to own them.
failures: Too many options; letting people skip essentials; choice with no guidance; choices only some people can take up
checks: Which choices really matter to people? What must stay the same for everyone?

name: Relevance and utility value
description: People see how the activity connects to their work, their goals or a situation they will face soon. It works better when they find the connection themselves than when they are told.
what: When people see what something is worth to them, they pay more attention and put in more effort.
basis: Eccles and Wigfield (2002), expectancy-value theory; Hulleman and Harackiewicz (2009), on asking learners to write about the relevance of what they learn.
methods: Live case; Action learning sets; Flipped learning
example: People bring a real conversation they have coming up in the next month and use the course tools to prepare it.
useful: Busy adults, mandatory courses and anyone who doubts the course is for them.
failures: Saying the content is important instead of showing it; relevance decided only by senior leaders; invented cases nobody recognises
checks: Can each person name a real use in the next 30 days? Is the link shown, not just claimed?

name: Curiosity and information gaps
description: The design shows people a gap between what they know and what they want to know, through a prediction, partial evidence or an unanswered question.
what: A gap that matters and can be closed draws attention and makes people want the answer.
basis: Loewenstein (1994), the information-gap theory of curiosity; Gruber, Gelman and Ranganath (2014), on how curiosity helps memory.
methods: Escape-room learning; Case method; Scenario-based learning
example: Show two sets of customer figures that seem to contradict each other. Teams must decide what they need to know before you hand out the next page of the case.
useful: Opening a session, investigations and problems people need to explore.
failures: Mystery for its own sake; holding back instructions people need; novelty that has nothing to do with the learning
checks: Does the gap matter, and does the activity close it?

name: Story and narrative transportation
description: Events, people, goals and consequences are told as a story, which helps people pay attention, make sense of it and remember it. People can also make decisions from inside a character's position.
what: A story gives facts an order and a cause, which makes them easier to follow and remember. People who are absorbed in a story are also more open to its point.
basis: Green and Brock (2000), on narrative transportation; Mar and colleagues (2021), a review of memory for stories compared with other text.
methods: Storytelling and case narrative; Critical incident method; Scenario-based learning
example: A case unfolds over a two-day course: the decisions teams make on day one come back as consequences on day two.
useful: Context, culture, ethics and decisions with emotional weight.
failures: Manipulating emotion; heroes and villains that oversimplify; a memorable story with no practice
checks: Does the story make the cause of each outcome clear? Where do people make decisions and review them?

name: Emotion and arousal regulation
description: Emotion directs attention and can make things memorable, but too much threat or stress narrows thinking. Good design creates real stakes while leaving people in control and giving them time to recover.
what: Some pressure helps people engage. Strong stress uses up the attention and working memory people need to think, and can make them avoid the situation in future.
basis: Tyng and colleagues (2017), a review of emotion and memory; Shields and colleagues (2016), a meta-analysis of the effects of stress on thinking; Keith and Frese (2005), on emotion control in error management training.
methods: Simulation-based training; Tabletop exercise; Role-play
example: A crisis exercise brings in a sudden press enquiry. Afterwards, everyone takes a two-minute pause before a calm debrief that starts with what people noticed, not who did badly.
useful: High-pressure work, building composure and emotionally demanding conversations.
failures: Humiliating people; manufactured panic; exposing people to distressing material without warning; constant intensity; assuming memorable means useful
checks: Is the emotional intensity needed, and in proportion? Are consent, another way to take part and recovery planned?

name: Embodied cognition
description: Movement, gesture, handling objects and arranging things in space become part of how people think and remember. Laying something out physically can make an abstract relationship visible.
what: Acting something out or arranging it in space gives people another way to understand and recall it, especially for steps and relationships.
basis: Engelkamp and Zimmer (1989), on the enactment effect, where acting out an instruction improves recall of it. Research on movement in adult workplace learning is thin, so treat this as a sensible design choice, not a proven effect.
methods: Walking learning / learning walk; Hands-on lab; Outdoor experiential learning
example: Teams place stakeholder cards on a table by influence and support, then move them as a case develops and explain each move.
useful: Systems, procedures, working together and seeing things from another position.
failures: Movement with no link to the content; activities some people cannot do; physical tasks that feel childish to the group
checks: What relationship does the physical action show? Is there an equal way to take part for people who cannot move about?

name: Reflection and consolidation
description: People look back at what happened, work out why, connect it to a model and decide what to change. Reflection also happens in the moment, when someone notices and adjusts while still doing the task. Pauses and sleep between hard practice give learning time to settle.
what: Thinking back over an experience turns it into a principle people can use again. Stopping briefly during a task to check how it is going lets people correct course while they still can. Rest between sessions helps memory settle.
basis: Di Stefano and colleagues (2014), on reflection after practice improving later performance; Tannenbaum and Cerasoli (2013), a meta-analysis of debriefs; Schön (1983), The Reflective Practitioner, on reflection in action.
methods: After-action review; Learning journal; Silent reflection / solo integration; Learning retrospective
example: Halfway through a negotiation role-play, everyone stops for one minute and writes what they think the other side wants and what they will try next. At the end of the day, each person writes one assumption that changed and one thing to test tomorrow.
useful: Making sense of complex experiences and turning them into something to use.
failures: Asking only how it felt; reflection that replaces practice; packed timetables with no time to think; interrupting so often the task never flows
checks: Does the reflection use evidence and end in a changed view or a next action?

name: Sleep and recovery
description: Enough sleep, breaks and recovery support attention, mood and memory. A multi-day programme can protect these, or wreck them by filling every hour.
what: New learning is strengthened during sleep and rest. Tiredness harms judgement and working memory, so a late night costs the next day's learning.
basis: Diekelmann and Born (2010), the memory function of sleep; Walker and Stickgold (2004), on sleep and the consolidation of skills.
methods: Residential learning retreat; Spaced practice
example: The hardest session ends by 17:00. Evening activities are optional, and the next morning starts with five minutes of recall on yesterday's key points.
useful: Multi-day programmes, demanding content and emotionally heavy practice.
failures: Compulsory late-night networking; bonding built around the bar; no breaks; treating exhaustion as commitment
checks: Does the timetable leave time for seven to nine hours' sleep and real breaks? Are evening activities optional?

name: Habit formation and cue design
description: A small action is tied to a reliable cue in the working day and repeated until it happens with little thought. The course can teach the action, but the cue and the repetition at work make the habit.
what: Repeating the same action in the same situation makes it more automatic over time. Habits form slowly and vary a lot between people.
basis: Lally and colleagues (2010), on how habits form in everyday life, a median of 66 days in their study; Wood and Neal (2007), on habits and goals.
methods: Job aids and in-tool guidance; Nudges and reminders; Learning in the flow of work
example: A three-question checklist appears automatically whenever someone opens a new client record, so the questions are asked at the moment they matter.
useful: Frequent, simple actions that should happen without much thought.
failures: Trying to make complex judgement a habit; cues that change from day to day; relying on willpower; too many new habits at once
checks: Is there a reliable cue and a small action? Has the work setting changed to support it?

name: Reinforcement and consequences
description: What happens after an action affects whether people repeat it. In learning, useful consequences include visible progress, harder challenges, recognition and real results.
what: People repeat actions that lead to outcomes they value, and timing matters. Rewards for the wrong thing, such as speed or clicks, teach the wrong thing.
basis: Skinner (1953), Science and Human Behavior; Deci, Koestner and Ryan (1999), a meta-analysis showing that some rewards reduce people's own interest in a task.
methods: Mastery learning; Serious game; Coaching
example: Teams unlock the harder case only after they show the basic moves in the first one, instead of earning points for finishing fastest.
useful: Consistent procedures, keeping going and simple actions you can observe.
failures: Game points that reward clicking through; prizes that crowd out interest in the task itself; rewarding speed over quality
checks: What behaviour is actually being rewarded? Is the reward fair and tied to quality?

name: Mastery learning
description: People move on only after showing they can do the thing to a set standard. Those who are not there yet get more teaching and another try. Time varies, the standard does not.
what: Clear standards, regular checks and a chance to correct stop gaps from piling up behind people.
basis: Bloom (1968), Learning for Mastery; Kulik, Kulik and Bangert-Drowns (1990), a meta-analysis of mastery learning programmes.
methods: Mastery learning; Mock assessment centre; Portfolio-based learning and assessment
example: Before the final client simulation, each person shows they can frame a client's problem accurately in a short check. Anyone not ready gets a 20-minute clinic and tries again.
useful: Knowledge that later steps depend on, and skills where mistakes are costly.
failures: Pass marks picked without reason; treating a quiz as proof of skill; no time or support to try again
checks: Is the standard observable and close to the real task? Is there real support and another attempt?

name: Assessment as learning
description: Assessment is designed so that preparing for it, doing it and acting on the feedback all teach, instead of only recording a result.
what: Recalling, performing and revising for an assessment strengthen what people know, and good criteria teach them what quality looks like.
basis: Black and Wiliam (1998), on formative assessment; Roediger and Karpicke (2006), the testing effect.
methods: Portfolio-based learning and assessment; Mock assessment centre; Practice clinic
example: Teams present a proposal to a panel who question them against the published criteria. They hand in a revised version the next day, with a note on what they changed and why.
useful: Bringing several skills together and showing progress.
failures: Assessment unrelated to the work; hidden criteria; a single attempt with no revision; scoring that punishes trying something new
checks: Does the assessment ask for the real performance? Does it produce feedback people act on?

name: Error management training
description: People are encouraged to explore, make safe mistakes, recover and learn how to handle errors. The aim is to get better at catching and fixing mistakes, not to prevent every one.
what: Errors show people how the system really works. Told that errors are useful, people try more and learn ways to recover that they can use at work.
basis: Keith and Frese (2008), a meta-analysis of 24 studies finding error management training beat error-avoidant training, especially for using skills in new situations.
methods: Hands-on lab; Simulation-based training; Tabletop exercise
example: People get a training copy of the finance system and a task with no step-by-step guide. They are told mistakes cost nothing here, and each error they hit is collected for the debrief on how to spot and undo it.
useful: Complex, changing work where mistakes cannot be ruled out.
failures: Mistakes that are unsafe or cannot be undone; blame; errors that teach nothing; no one showing how to recover
checks: Are the errors safe and contained? Do people practise spotting, reporting and recovering?

name: Attention and signalling
description: The design points people's limited attention at what matters most: the key cue, the relationship or the change. Signals can be visual, spoken or a pause, and should fade as people gain expertise.
what: People can only take in a little at once, so what they attend to is what they learn. Signals cut the search and help beginners see where to look.
basis: Mayer (2020), Multimedia Learning, on the signalling principle; Schneider and colleagues (2018), a meta-analysis of signals in multimedia learning.
methods: Interactive video; Interactive lecture; Expert think-aloud
example: Pause a recorded meeting just before the client's small sign of resistance and ask: "What did you notice in the last ten seconds?"
useful: Beginners learning where to look and what matters.
failures: Highlighting everything; signals that give the answer away for good; decorative animation
checks: Are the signals few and tied to what people must notice? Are they removed as people improve?

name: Identity-based learning
description: Learning helps people see themselves as capable members of a profession, take on its standards and tell the story of their own development.
what: How people see themselves at work affects what they try, how long they keep going and whose feedback they accept.
basis: Wenger (1998), Communities of Practice; Ibarra (1999), on how people try out professional identities in a new role.
methods: Apprenticeship; Mentoring; Community of practice; Portfolio-based learning and assessment
example: New trainers keep a portfolio of sessions they have designed and run, and present one piece of work and their next step to their community of practice each quarter.
useful: Moving into a new role, leadership and new professions.
failures: Pushing an identity on people; hero worship; one approved style; new branding with no change in practice
checks: What practice are people joining? Can they see more than one way to belong to it?
